investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 34-year-old woman is referred with a new firm, non-tender 2 cm breast lump. Which imaging modality should be first-line as part of her triple assessment?
options: No imaging is needed if the lump feels benign
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: In women under 40 the breast tissue is dense and poorly assessed by mammography, so ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality. Mammography is preferred at ≥40 and for screening. MRI and CT are not routine first-line breast investigations.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 52-year-old woman undergoes triple assessment for a hard, irregular lump. Examination is P5 and mammography is M5, but the core biopsy is reported as B2 (benign). What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge as the biopsy is benign
Repeat the assessment in one year
Arrange repeat/excision biopsy because the results are discordant
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.answer: Arrange repeat/excision biopsy because the results are discordant
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: A benign biopsy that conflicts with a highly suspicious examination and imaging is discordant. Discordance mandates further assessment (repeat core biopsy or diagnostic excision). A single benign arm never overrides clinical and radiological suspicion of malignancy.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: Which of the following best explains why core biopsy is preferred over fine-needle aspiration cytology in triple assessment?
options: It is less painful for the patient
It provides histology, distinguishing invasive from in-situ disease, and gives receptor status
It can be performed without imaging guidance
It avoids the need for clinical examination
It is the only test that can be scored 1–5
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.answer: It provides histology, distinguishing invasive from in-situ disease, and gives receptor status
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: Core biopsy yields a tissue architecture (histology) sample, allowing invasive cancer to be distinguished from DCIS, and enables ER/PR/HER2 receptor testing to guide management. FNA gives cytology only. Both can be scored 1–5, so that is not the distinguishing advantage.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to her GP. Which single feature most clearly warrants an urgent (2-week-wait) breast clinic referral for triple assessment?
options: Bilateral milky nipple discharge on expression
Longstanding stable smooth mobile lump unchanged for 5 years
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: Unilateral bloody nipple discharge is a red-flag symptom requiring urgent 2-week-wait referral. Bilateral cyclical tenderness/lumpiness and bilateral milky discharge are typically benign/physiological, and a longstanding unchanged mobile lump is low-risk.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with a firm, mobile, painless breast lump. Which imaging modality is most appropriate as first-line investigation?
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: In women under 40 the breast tissue is dense and radiodense, reducing mammographic sensitivity, so USS is first-line. It also avoids ionising radiation. Mammography becomes primary imaging in those ≥40. MRI, CT and PET-CT are not first-line for a discrete lump.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 34-year-old woman has a breast USS showing an oval, well-defined, hypoechoic mass that is wider-than-tall with a thin capsule. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: A well-defined, smooth, oval, wider-than-tall (parallel), hypoechoic mass with a thin capsule is the classic benign appearance of a fibroadenoma. Malignant lesions are typically taller-than-wide, irregular and spiculated with posterior acoustic shadowing. DCIS is characterised by microcalcification best seen on mammography.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 30-year-old woman with a clinically suspicious hard, tethered breast lump has a USS reported as showing only benign-appearing changes. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Proceed with core biopsy as part of triple assessment
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.answer: Proceed with core biopsy as part of triple assessment
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: A normal or benign USS does not exclude malignancy when clinical suspicion persists. Triple assessment (clinical exam + imaging + histology) must be completed, so core biopsy is indicated. Discharge or delayed re-scan risks missing cancer; empirical tamoxifen and PET-CT are inappropriate without a tissue diagnosis.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 62-year-old woman is recalled from routine NHS breast screening. Her mammogram shows a cluster of fine pleomorphic microcalcifications in the left upper outer quadrant, with no discrete mass and a normal ultrasound. What is the most appropriate next step to obtain tissue?
options: Reassure and return to routine 3-yearly screening
Excisional biopsy of the whole quadrant
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: Pleomorphic clustered microcalcification is the hallmark of DCIS and is often invisible on ultrasound, so US-guided biopsy is not possible. Sampling requires stereotactic/mammographic guidance. Ignoring it or delaying with a repeat film would miss a potential malignancy, and excisional biopsy is not the first tissue step.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 33-year-old woman presents with a firm, irregular breast lump. Ultrasound and core biopsy are arranged. Why is mammography NOT the preferred first-line imaging in this patient?
options: Mammography is contraindicated in all symptomatic women
Dense breast tissue in young women reduces mammographic sensitivity, and it carries a radiation dose
Ultrasound is more sensitive for microcalcification
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.answer: Dense breast tissue in young women reduces mammographic sensitivity, and it carries a radiation dose
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: In women under 40 the breast is denser, lowering mammographic sensitivity, and mammography involves a small radiation dose — so USS is first-line. Mammography is actually the modality best at detecting microcalcification (not the reverse), which excludes the other options.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 48-year-old woman has a clinically suspicious breast lump. Mammography is reported as normal (M1). What is the most appropriate management?
options: Discharge, as the mammogram excludes cancer
Proceed to ultrasound and biopsy to complete triple assessment
Refer directly for wide local excision
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.answer: Proceed to ultrasound and biopsy to complete triple assessment
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: A normal mammogram does not exclude cancer, particularly in dense breasts, and clinical suspicion overrides a negative image. Triple assessment must be completed with USS ± biopsy. Discharging or delaying risks missing malignancy, and treatment is not started before histological diagnosis.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 44-year-old woman reports spontaneous blood-stained discharge from a single duct of her right nipple. Examination reveals no mass. Ultrasound and mammography are unremarkable, but the discharge is confirmed positive for blood. Ductography shows a smooth rounded filling defect within a dilated subareolar duct. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: A smooth, rounded intraductal filling defect on ductography in the context of single-duct bloody discharge is the classic appearance of an intraductal papilloma, the commonest benign cause of bloody nipple discharge. DCIS/carcinoma tends to give an irregular defect or duct cut-off and must be excluded, but the smooth defect here favours papilloma.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: Which of the following features of nipple discharge is most concerning and warrants urgent 2-week-wait referral?
options: Multi-duct green discharge only on squeezing
Clear discharge from multiple ducts of both breasts
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: Worrying features are unilateral, single-duct, spontaneous, blood-stained discharge, an associated mass, or age >50 — these require urgent referral and triple assessment. Bilateral, multi-duct, expression-only, milky (galactorrhoea) or green/creamy (duct ectasia) discharge is reassuring.

investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.question: A 51-year-old woman has persistent spontaneous bloody discharge from a single duct. Triple assessment including ultrasound is unremarkable and no lesion is localised. What is the most appropriate next step that is both diagnostic and therapeutic?
investigations__BREAST__Triple Assessmen.explanation: Persistent pathological single-duct discharge with a normal triple assessment is investigated with microdochectomy (or total duct excision), which excises the affected duct and provides tissue for histology — it is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Discharge cytology is of limited value, and prolactin is relevant to bilateral milky galactorrhoea, not unilateral bloody discharge.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A 58-year-old woman has a spiculated mass on mammography. Ultrasound-guided core biopsy shows invasive ductal carcinoma. Which single advantage does core biopsy have over fine-needle aspiration cytology in this setting?
options: It is less painful for the patient
It carries no risk of bleeding or infection
It distinguishes invasive carcinoma from in situ disease and allows receptor testing
It can be performed without imaging guidance
It provides an immediate result at the bedside
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: It distinguishes invasive carcinoma from in situ disease and allows receptor testing
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: Core biopsy preserves tissue architecture (histology), so it separates invasive cancer from DCIS, grades the tumour and provides tissue for ER/PR/HER2 immunohistochemistry. FNA yields only cytology and cannot do this. The other options are not genuine advantages of core biopsy over FNA.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A 45-year-old pre-menopausal woman is diagnosed with an ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-negative invasive breast cancer. Which systemic therapy is most appropriate to target her tumour biology?
options: An aromatase inhibitor such as anastrozole
Chemotherapy alone with no hormonal therapy
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: Hormone-receptor-positive tumours respond to endocrine therapy. In a pre-menopausal woman the standard agent is tamoxifen; aromatase inhibitors are used in post-menopausal women (they are ineffective as monotherapy in functioning ovaries). Trastuzumab/pertuzumab target HER2, which is negative here.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A core biopsy of a breast lesion is reported as HER2 equivocal (IHC 2+). What is the correct next step to determine HER2 status?
options: Report the tumour as HER2-positive and start trastuzumab
Reflex the sample to in-situ hybridisation (ISH/FISH) for gene amplification
Repeat the ER and PR immunohistochemistry
Proceed directly to surgical excision for definitive HER2 testing
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: Reflex the sample to in-situ hybridisation (ISH/FISH) for gene amplification
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: HER2 IHC is scored 0/1+ (negative), 3+ (positive) and 2+ (equivocal). An equivocal 2+ result is reflexed to ISH/FISH to assess HER2 gene amplification, which resolves whether the tumour is truly HER2-positive and eligible for anti-HER2 therapy.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A 52-year-old woman has a firm 2 cm breast lump. Ultrasound-guided sampling is planned and the MDT wants to know whether the cancer is invasive or in situ and to obtain ER/PR/HER2 status. Which investigation is required to answer both questions?
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: Core biopsy provides tissue architecture, so it can distinguish invasive from in-situ (DCIS) disease and allows immunohistochemistry for ER/PR/HER2. FNA gives cytology (cells only) and cannot reliably do either, which is why core biopsy has largely replaced it as the pathology arm of triple assessment.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with a smooth, mobile breast lump. FNA yields 15 mL of green fluid and the lump completely disappears afterwards. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure the patient; no cytology needed
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: Reassure the patient; no cytology needed
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: Non-bloodstained (clear/straw/green) fluid with complete resolution of the lump indicates a benign simple cyst. Cytology is not required. Fluid is only sent, and further imaging/biopsy arranged, if the fluid is bloodstained, a residual mass persists, or the cyst recurs.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: An FNA of a breast lump is reported as C1. What does this indicate?
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: In the C1-C5 cytology system, C1 means the specimen is inadequate (acellular or non-diagnostic) and must be repeated. C2 is benign, C3 atypia probably benign, C4 suspicious, and C5 malignant. FNA has a higher inadequate rate than core biopsy.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A 58-year-old woman with a newly diagnosed invasive ductal carcinoma undergoes staging axillary ultrasound. A node shows cortical thickening of 5 mm and loss of the fatty hilum. USS-guided core biopsy confirms metastatic adenocarcinoma. What is the most appropriate management of her axilla?
options: Sentinel lymph node biopsy at the time of surgery
Axillary lymph node clearance (or axillary radiotherapy)
MRI of the axilla to confirm staging
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: Axillary lymph node clearance (or axillary radiotherapy)
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: Biopsy-proven nodal metastasis means the axilla is already known to be involved, so the patient proceeds directly to definitive axillary treatment (clearance or radiotherapy). A sentinel node biopsy is unnecessary because it would only be used to detect occult disease that is already confirmed.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A 46-year-old woman with a 2 cm breast cancer has a pre-operative axillary ultrasound reported as normal, with all nodes showing thin cortices and preserved fatty hila. What is the correct next step for staging her axilla?
options: Proceed straight to axillary lymph node clearance
No axillary staging is required as USS was normal
Sentinel lymph node biopsy at the time of primary surgery
USS-guided fine-needle aspiration of the largest node
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: Sentinel lymph node biopsy at the time of primary surgery
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: A normal axillary USS does not exclude micrometastasis, so sentinel lymph node biopsy is still required at surgery to detect occult nodal disease. Proceeding to clearance would be over-treatment, and no staging at all would risk missing occult metastases.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: During staging of a breast cancer patient, which single ultrasound feature is most suggestive that an axillary lymph node harbours metastatic disease?
options: A thin uniform cortex of 2 mm
Cortical thickening greater than 3 mm with loss of the fatty hilum
A node with a preserved reniform (kidney-bean) shape
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: Cortical thickening greater than 3 mm with loss of the fatty hilum
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: Metastatic infiltration expands the cortex and effaces the fatty hilum, so cortical thickening >3 mm with loss of the hilum is the classic suspicious appearance. An oval node with a thin cortex, bright fatty hilum, and reniform shape are all normal features.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A 58-year-old woman has a 15 mm invasive ductal carcinoma. Axillary examination is normal and ultrasound shows no abnormal nodes. She is scheduled for wide local excision. What is the most appropriate method to stage her axilla?
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: She has early breast cancer with a clinically and ultrasound node-negative axilla — the exact indication for SLNB. It stages the axilla accurately with far less morbidity than upfront clearance. Clearance is reserved for biopsy-proven node-positive disease or a positive sentinel node.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: During a sentinel lymph node biopsy, which combination is most commonly used to identify the sentinel node?
options: Methylene blue dye and iodinated CT contrast
Patent blue dye and technetium-99m radioisotope with a gamma probe
Indocyanine green and gadolinium MRI contrast
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: Patent blue dye and technetium-99m radioisotope with a gamma probe
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: Dual localisation uses patent blue dye plus radioisotope (Tc-99m) injected around the tumour/areola; the sentinel node appears blue and/or is detected as 'hot' by a gamma probe, then excised for histology. This dual technique maximises sentinel node identification.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A patient's pre-operative ultrasound-guided core biopsy of an axillary node confirms metastatic breast carcinoma. What is the most appropriate axillary procedure at surgery?
options: Repeat sentinel node biopsy with blue dye only
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: SLNB is only for the node-NEGATIVE axilla. When nodes are already biopsy-proven positive, staging by SLNB is unnecessary and the patient proceeds directly to axillary lymph node clearance (or, in selected cases, axillary radiotherapy as an alternative to clearance).

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A 55-year-old woman has a 3 cm invasive ductal carcinoma with 2 axillary lymph nodes involved and a histological grade of 2. What is her Nottingham Prognostic Index?
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: NPI = (0.2 × 3) + nodal score + grade score = 0.6 + 2 (1–3 nodes) + 2 (Grade 2) = 4.6, placing her in the moderate prognostic band (3.41–5.4).

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: The Nottingham (modified Scarff–Bloom–Richardson) grading system sums three histological components. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: None of the above (all three named are components)
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: The three SBR components are tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism and mitotic count, each scored 1–3. Lymphovascular invasion is a separate prognostic factor and is not part of the grade score.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A tumour has an NPI of 6.2. Which statement best reflects its prognosis and management implication?
options: Good prognosis (~85–90% 5-yr survival); chemotherapy rarely indicated
Moderate prognosis (~70%); hormone therapy alone is sufficient
Poor prognosis (~50% 5-yr survival); stronger case for adjuvant chemotherapy
Good prognosis; no further MDT discussion needed
The NPI cannot exceed 5.4, so the value must be an error
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: Poor prognosis (~50% 5-yr survival); stronger case for adjuvant chemotherapy
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: An NPI >5.4 falls in the poor prognostic band (~50% 5-year survival) and, together with high grade, supports a stronger indication for adjuvant chemotherapy, decided at MDT with receptor and gene-expression data.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A 58-year-old woman has a 15 mm invasive ductal carcinoma that is ER-positive, HER2-negative and lymph-node-negative. Her PREDICT/NPI risk is intermediate and the MDT is unsure whether to add chemotherapy to endocrine therapy. What is the single most appropriate next step to inform this decision?
options: Proceed directly to adjuvant chemotherapy plus endocrine therapy
Perform a gene-expression profiling assay (e.g. Oncotype DX) to predict chemotherapy benefit
Give endocrine therapy alone and arrange no further testing
Request BRCA1/BRCA2 germline testing to decide on chemotherapy
Repeat the core biopsy to reassess tumour grade
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: Perform a gene-expression profiling assay (e.g. Oncotype DX) to predict chemotherapy benefit
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: She fits the eligible group precisely: early ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative disease with an uncertain (intermediate-risk) chemotherapy decision. A gene-expression assay estimates recurrence risk and predicts chemotherapy benefit, allowing chemo to be added only if the score is high. BRCA testing and re-biopsy do not answer the chemo-benefit question, and committing to either chemo or endocrine therapy alone without the score wastes the tool's value.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: A patient's Oncotype DX assay returns a LOW Recurrence Score for her ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative breast cancer. What does this result most directly indicate for management?
options: High risk of recurrence, so escalate to chemotherapy plus endocrine therapy
Very low predicted chemotherapy benefit, so endocrine therapy alone is appropriate
A need for trastuzumab because HER2 status is now positive
That surgery should be avoided in favour of chemotherapy alone
That the tumour is triple-negative and needs urgent chemotherapy
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: Very low predicted chemotherapy benefit, so endocrine therapy alone is appropriate
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: A low score corresponds to a low risk of distant recurrence and, importantly, very little benefit from adding chemotherapy. The correct action is endocrine therapy alone, sparing the patient chemotherapy toxicity — the principle of de-escalation supported by TAILORx. The score does not alter HER2 status or the role of surgery.

investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.question: For which one of the following patients is gene-expression profiling (Oncotype DX / EndoPredict) LEAST appropriate to guide the chemotherapy decision?
options: A woman with early ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative cancer and intermediate clinical risk
A postmenopausal woman with ER-positive, HER2-negative disease and one micrometastatic node
A woman with a triple-negative (ER-, PR-, HER2-) invasive carcinoma
A woman with ER-positive, HER2-negative cancer where the MDT is genuinely uncertain about chemotherapy
A woman with a small ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative tumour of intermediate grade
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.answer: A woman with a triple-negative (ER-, PR-, HER2-) invasive carcinoma
investigations__BREAST__Pathology & Stag.explanation: Gene-expression assays are validated in and reserved for ER-positive, HER2-negative disease where the chemotherapy decision is uncertain. Triple-negative cancer (like HER2-positive disease) has its own clear chemotherapy indication and the assays are not used or validated in it — a low score must never be used to withhold chemotherapy in these patients. All the other options describe the eligible ER-positive/HER2-negative group.
